subject: business-management
title: Ora Milling: Capital and revenue expenditure
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Ora Milling: Ora buys a new grain mill for USD 90000 and pays USD 2400 for its routine monthly servicing. The servicing does not extend the mill’s expected useful life.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the term capital expenditure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish capital expenditure from revenue expenditure using two items in the case of Ora Milling.

steps.text: Spending to acquire or improve non-current assets
expected to benefit the organization over more than one accounting period.
The mill purchase is capital expenditure.
It acquires an asset used over several years.
The USD 90000 supports future milling rather than just this month’s activity.
Routine servicing is revenue expenditure.
It maintains current operations without adding a long-term improvement.
The USD 2400 belongs to the current period’s operating costs.

title: Avo Panels: total and average cost
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Avo Panels makes insulation panels. Monthly fixed costs are USD 48,000; variable cost is USD 14 per unit. It produces 6,000 units in the month. Within this output range, fixed costs and variable cost per unit remain unchanged. Show workings and give money to two decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate total monthly cost.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate average cost per unit.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a higher output does not necessarily increase profit.

steps.text: Fixed cost + variable cost per unit × output = 48000+14×6000.
Total cost / output = 132000/6000.
USD 22.00 per unit.
Higher output can spread fixed cost over more units.
But producing units does not prove they can be sold.
If demand is insufficient, inventory and storage costs can rise without equivalent revenue.
The selling price and achievable sales volume are needed before concluding that profit increases.

verification.method: Syllabus/AO scope check; independent arithmetic and case-reasoning review; analytic/best-fit allocation audit

title: Uvo Sensors: returns on expansion
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Uvo Sensors supplies sensors. Current annual profit before interest and tax is USD 78,000; equity is USD 300,000; non-current liabilities are USD 90,000. An expansion would produce forecast annual profit before interest and tax of USD 90,000 with total capital employed of USD 500,000. These are comparable full-year estimates. Use the stated capital-employed bases without averaging. Show workings; percentages to two decimals.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate current ROCE using equity plus non-current liabilities as capital employed.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate forecast ROCE after expansion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the financial data, recommend whether Uvo Sensors should undertake the expansion.

steps.text: Indicative support: Annual profit before interest and tax rises from USD 78,000 to USD 90,000
Indicative counterargument: Capital employed rises and ROCE changes from 20.00% to 18.00%; extra profit must justify the extra investment

One defensible judgment: Compare forecast ROCE with the cost and risk of capital and strategic benefits; higher absolute profit alone does not settle the choice. Alternative recommendations earn full credit when supported by the case and a coherent response to the counterargument.

Evidence limitation: The forecast’s reliability, cost of capital, cash-flow timing and non-financial benefits are not given. Explain how this uncertainty affects confidence in the decision. Apply best fit: a theoretical-only answer can earn at most 4; without an explained case/stimulus limitation at most 8. Do not require all indicative points or award them separately.

bands.descriptor: No relevant response.
Limited relevant knowledge of the proposed expansion; arguments are mainly assertions and application to Uvo Sensors is absent or superficial.
Some accurate business knowledge and explanation of the proposed expansion, but application or analysis is limited and the answer is largely one-sided.

Relevant concepts are used to analyse the proposed expansion with some meaningful application to Uvo Sensors. Some opposing considerations are identified, but their relative importance or the recommendation is only partly supported.

Accurate relevant theory supports balanced, developed analysis of the proposed expansion using the specific circumstances of Uvo Sensors. The recommendation follows from the arguments and recognizes a condition or stakeholder trade-off.

Focused, balanced analysis integrates relevant business theory with the evidence about Uvo Sensors; competing consequences and their relative significance are evaluated. The recommendation is convincing and conditional, addresses an identified weakness, and explains a material limitation of the available evidence.

verification.method: Syllabus/AO scope check; independent arithmetic and case-reasoning review; analytic/best-fit allocation audit
verification.notes: Family bm49-roce. CurrentCE=390000;ROCE=20.00000000%;forecast=18.00000000%. Forecast not treated as guaranteed or compared solely on absolute profit.

title: Mro Labs: labour turnover
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Mro Labs employed 72 people on the first day and 88 on the last day of the year. 12 employees left during the year. Estimate average employment as the arithmetic mean of these two counts. Direct recruitment and induction cost is USD 3,600 per replacement. Assume every leaver is replaced once; exclude lost output and other indirect costs. Show workings.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate annual labour turnover, using average employment. Give the percentage to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the direct replacement cost if every leaver is replaced once.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of concluding that the turnover rate proves employees are poorly motivated.

steps.text: Average employment=(72+88)/2=80; turnover=12/80 × 100.
Turnover records departures rather than motives.
Some leavers may retire or relocate despite being satisfied.
An exit survey would be needed before attributing all departures to motivation.
An annual average can conceal timing or departmental differences.
A short restructuring or one problematic department may account for many departures.
The whole-workforce percentage alone cannot locate the problem or identify the appropriate intervention.

verification.notes: Family bm34-labour-turnover. Average=80.0; leavers/average*100=15.000000%; direct replacement=43200. Recruitment and labour turnover are explicitly HL-only 2.4.

stem:

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

steps.text: A theory that motivation depends on believing effort can lead to performance
performance will lead to a reward, and that reward is valued.

Harder territories may require more effort for the same bonus.
Experienced staff may reduce effort if they view Cru’s reward ratio as inequitable.
Relevant comparisons need not be objectively identical.
Cru’s staff judge rewards against colleagues with easier territories.
A clear explanation and review of territory difficulty may matter more than a uniform bonus increase.

title: Wali Delivery: decision tree
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Wali considers launching a cargo-bike route rather than retaining its existing van route. The launch costs USD 12,000 now. The probability estimates are managerial judgments. Show workings and give monetary answers to two decimal places.

title: Hesto Audio: Porter: differentiation and focus
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Hesto Audio: Hesto makes repairable amplifiers for touring musicians. A mass retailer requests sealed low-price units. Current users pay for durable connectors and quick field repair.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the term differentiation focus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for Hesto Audio of pursuing differentiation focus using Porter’s generic strategies.

parts.label: c

steps.text: A strategy offering distinctive value to a narrow target segment
to secure preference or a premium rather than serving the whole market on lowest cost.
Advantage: Repairability differentiates the offer.
Applied consequence: professional touring users may value reduced downtime enough to pay a premium.
Disadvantage: Focused demand limits volume.
Applied consequence: few large touring customers could create volatile orders.
Indicative support: Repairability differentiates the offer because professional touring users may value reduced downtime enough to pay a premium
Indicative counterargument: Focused demand limits volume because few large touring customers could create volatile orders

One defensible judgment: Keep professional differentiation if lifetime service margins support it; do not dilute repairability without a separate market proposition. Alternative recommendations earn full credit when supported by the case and a coherent response to the counterargument.

Evidence limitation: Customer replacement cycles and expected service costs are not supplied. Explain how this uncertainty affects confidence in the decision. title: Isto Access: three-year social-enterprise plan
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Isto Access is a for-profit social enterprise supplying a subscription cargo-tricycle lending service. It reinvests surplus to address affordable mobility for isolated adults.

Resource 1 — founder’s note: The enterprise must retain affordable access while becoming financially self-sustaining over the next three years.

Resource 2 — finance report: Available unrestricted cash is USD 28,000. The proposed expansion would use USD 24,000 immediately. Current monthly net cash outflow is USD 2000. There is no agreed borrowing facility.

Resource 3 — service log: Repairs take three weeks and members miss work. Users value reliable access more than additional locations.

Resource 4 — staff discussion: The team supports training two local repairers and opening one additional lending hub, but needs training time and clear responsibilities. Existing staff cannot safely absorb further duties.

Resource 5 — funder message: A restricted grant of USD 12000 is available for staff training only; it cannot pay rent, stock or the expansion. A decision and implementation schedule are required within two months.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using an appropriate business management theory, describe one human need addressed by the social enterprise.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two challenges facing the social enterprise.

parts.label: c

steps.text: Maslow: safety, belonging or esteem needs can be linked to dependable mobility and participation.
Link the need to affordable mobility for isolated adults; the response must describe the need addressed by the service, not merely name the enterprise.
A liquidity challenge exists.
Spending nearly all unrestricted cash leaves too little to meet recurring obligations.
Only USD 4000 remains after expansion, enough for two months at the stated USD 2000 monthly outflow; the training grant cannot fund those bills.
A staffing/operational challenge exists.
Training and responsibilities must improve reliability before further expansion increases demands.
Repairs take three weeks and members miss work; using existing staff without protected training time could worsen the specific service problem.

A defensible plan first protects a cash reserve and delays the immediate expansion: USD 28,000 unrestricted cash must fund existing outflows and operating needs; the USD 12000 restricted grant is not interchangeable with that cash. Evaluate finance–operations–HR trade-offs: delaying expansion protects liquidity and reliability but postpones access for new users; training improves long-term service while temporarily consuming staff time. title: Cya Bags: interpreting positioning
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Cya Bags studies the market for day bags. The map uses average customer ratings from 1 (low) to 10 (high) for perceived price and quality. A, B and C are existing competing offers; New is the proposed offer. Ratings are perceptions, not measured technical performance or actual prices.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the term position map.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the intended positioning of New relative to A and B.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one limitation of using this map alone to decide whether to launch New.

steps.text: A visual representation of customers’ perceptions of competing products
plotted against selected attributes such as perceived price and quality.
New is perceived as cheaper than A.
Its similar high perceived quality suggests a value-for-money position relative to A.
New is perceived as higher-quality and higher-priced than B.
It therefore does not compete solely on the lowest price against B.
Perceptions do not directly measure purchase intentions or segment size.
An apparently empty position may reflect low demand rather than an opportunity.
The two attributes omit other benefits such as convenience, durability or service.
Research on target customers and costs is required before treating the position as commercially viable.

verification.method: Syllabus/AO scope check; independent arithmetic and case-reasoning review; analytic/best-fit allocation audit
verification.notes: Family bm64-position-map. Points=[('A', 8, 8), ('B', 3, 4), ('C', 7, 3), ('New', 5, 8)]; New price betweenAandB; New quality nearA aboveB. Axes explicitly perceptions; no inference of segment size from unoccupied space.

stem:

title: Aza Events: critical path and float
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Aza Events plans a venue launch. The activity-on-arrow network is supplied; arrows run from the lower-numbered event to the higher-numbered event. Durations are in days. An event occurs only after every incoming activity finishes. Activities may run in parallel, resources are unconstrained for the calculation, and the project starts at time 0. parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total float and free float of activity B. Show both calculations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of treating this minimum duration as a guaranteed completion date.

steps.text: Compare A+C+E=11 with B+D+E=7.
Critical path A–C–E; duration 11 days.
Total float=latest finish event−earliest start event−duration=7−0−3.
Total float=4 days.
Free float=earliest finish event−earliest start event−duration=3−0−3.
Free float=0 days.
Durations are estimates.
A critical activity taking longer can delay the entire completion date.
Managers need monitoring and contingency rather than assuming the calculated date is certain.
The network assumes resources can support parallel activities.
Shared staff or equipment may make the displayed overlap impossible.
Resource constraints must be checked before adopting the theoretical minimum schedule.

title: Eza Meals: Crisis and contingency planning
stem:
All organizations and data in this question are fictional.

Eza Meals: Eza supplies chilled meals. A backup generator and alternate cold store would cost USD 18000 yearly. Power failures are infrequent but a long outage could spoil meals and interrupt vulnerable customers’ deliveries.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the term contingency planning.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for Eza Meals of funding the proposed contingency plan.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the case information and relevant business management theory, recommend whether Eza Meals should proceed with funding the proposed contingency plan.

steps.text: Preparing in advance for possible disruptive events
by identifying risks, responsibilities and fallback actions before a crisis occurs.
Advantage: Prepared backup can reduce disruption and safety risk.
Applied consequence: Eza can protect food and deliveries during an outage.
Disadvantage: The plan uses scarce funds even when no outage occurs.
Applied consequence: USD 18000 cannot also be spent on routine service improvements.
Indicative support: Prepared backup can reduce disruption and safety risk because Eza can protect food and deliveries during an outage
Indicative counterargument: The plan uses scarce funds even when no outage occurs because USD 18000 cannot also be spent on routine service improvements

One defensible judgment: Fund proportionate backup after risk assessment and test responsibilities; compare shared storage options rather than treating all safeguards as equally necessary. Alternative recommendations earn full credit when supported by the case and a coherent response to the counterargument.

Evidence limitation: The probability and financial or human impact of a long outage are uncertain. Explain how this uncertainty affects confidence in the decision. Apply best fit: a theoretical-only answer can earn at most 4; without an explained case/stimulus limitation at most 8. Do not require all indicative points or award them separately.

Sza Tools considers introducing a shared quality system. A management workshop assigns scores from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong). The scores are judgments, not measured probabilities.

| Driving force | Score | Restraining force | Score |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Fewer defects | 4 | Blame concerns | 5 |
| Common information | 4 | Training time | 2 |

Management proposes a no-blame pilot and funded training before implementation. Show workings for totals and apply the analysis to the case.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the total driving score and total restraining score.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a no-blame pilot and funded training could reduce resistance to this operational change.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of using only the force-field totals to approve the change.

steps.text: Driving=4+4; restraining=5+2.
Driving=8; restraining=7.
Addressing a restraining force can improve acceptance without simply increasing pressure.
The proposed a no-blame pilot and funded training directly addresses the stated concerns about capability, cost or implementation.
It can give employees practical evidence that the operational change is manageable.
Managers should check whether the intervention actually reduces the relevant concern rather than assume a lower score.
Scores are subjective judgments.
Different employees may assign different importance to the same force.
The apparent numerical balance is not an objective probability of success.
Adding scores assumes forces can be compared and offset directly.
A critical safety or feasibility constraint cannot always be cancelled by several small benefits.
Management must investigate the underlying issues rather than approve a change solely from the higher total.

verification.method: Syllabus/AO scope check; independent arithmetic and case-reasoning review; analytic/best-fit allocation audit
verification.notes: Family bm100-force-field. Drivingtotal=8;restrainingtotal=7; scores not treated as statisticaldata, guaranteeddecision or additiveprobabilities.
